overview: Alsea communities lived along the central Oregon coast, with villages around the Alsea River and Cape Perpetua. Their history survives through community knowledge, language records, ethnographic testimony and the continuing Siletz confederation.

periods.title: The Coast Reservation and subagency
periods.summary: The Coast Reservation was established in 1855. The Alsea Subagency brought Alsea communities and people forcibly removed from other homelands under an intrusive colonial administration.

periods.title: Loss of protected land and contested removal
periods.summary: Congress opened the southern reservation section to settlers in 1875. Officials sought further removals, but community opposition and disputes over funding complicated their plans. Relocation did not happen everywhere at once.

periods.title: Recording language and remembered lifeways
periods.summary: Named speakers contributed stories, translations and descriptions of everyday life to researchers. Written texts and later sound recordings preserve different kinds of evidence, shaped by the circumstances of collection.

periods.title: Termination of federal recognition
periods.summary: The Siletz Tribe dates the effect of the 1954 federal termination law to 1956. The loss of recognition and services changed its legal relationship with the United States; it did not end the people.

periods.title: Restored recognition and continuing community
periods.summary: The 1977 Restoration Act restored federal recognition and eligibility for tribal services. Alsea remain among the peoples represented in the Siletz confederation, whose government provides community programs.

items.text: The Cape Perpetua area offered several kinds of food. Families hunted and fished, while the intertidal zone supplied clams and mussels. Villages near the cape, Seal Rock and the Alsea estuary connected people to these resources. Coastal life depended on knowing different environments, not on a single food source.

In accounts recorded by Drucker, women prepared salmon with shell knives and preserved it through drying and smoke. Stored fish hung in baskets or bundles inside winter houses, where warmth helped protect it from damp. Harvesting a seasonal run required skilled processing and storage to feed households later.

Winter houses were described as rectangular excavated spaces lined with cedar planks, with posts supporting overlapping roof boards. Larger houses accommodated several families, each with its own space and hearth. These are remembered construction practices recorded from speakers, not a newly excavated building assigned to a precise ancient year.

Leona Ludson of Siletz supplied much of Drucker’s account, supplemented by John Albert of Oakville. Their conversations took place in 1933 and appeared in print in 1939. Identifying these contributors makes clear that the publication depended on Indigenous expertise, even though the anthropologist organized and interpreted the resulting text.

The introduction to Alsea Texts and Myths names Alsea George and U. S. Grant as contributors to Livingston Farrand’s 1900 collection. William Smith and Thomas Jackson later worked with Frachtenberg, mainly in 1910 and again in 1913. The 1920 book therefore brings together several people’s contributions made at different times.

Frachtenberg also explained that he revised Farrand’s notes with help from his own contributors because their sound-writing systems differed. He reworked translations and paragraphing. The printed stories are valuable language records, but their presentation reflects choices by speakers, translators and editors rather than an untouched transcript of one conversation.

A Smithsonian finding aid describes an aluminum disc recorded by John Paul Marr with John Albert in May 1941 at Oakville. Cataloged as NAA INV.00000550, it includes Albert’s Bear and Wren story in English and vocabulary in Alsea and English. This preserves a different documentary medium from the earlier printed collection.

Patricia Whereat Phillips traced different forms of Cape Perpetua’s name in Alsea, Hanis and Lower Umpqua. She consulted linguist Eugene Buckley about a possible meaning related to an open or exposed place. Her discussion keeps the proposal tentative: John Albert preserved the Alsea name without giving its meaning.

The Siletz tribal history challenges descriptions of land around Yaquina Bay as empty when it was opened to settlers in 1865. It identifies Alsea and other Indigenous families living and farming there, then being displaced from homes and fields. The account links the change in reservation boundaries to losses in daily subsistence.

An 1875 council transcript reproduced by historian David G. Lewis records Coos leader Jack Rogers resisting another removal from the Alsea area. Rogers stressed homes people had built and nearby food supplies. He was a Coos representative living in the subagency, not an Alsea chief; the distinction reveals the different peoples forced together there.

Lewis compares removal orders with agents’ letters about unavailable funds, competing plans and negotiations. His study places the move from the former Alsea Reservation toward Salmon River at least as late as 1878. An order issued in 1875 cannot therefore be treated as proof that every family moved that year.

The 1977 Siletz Restoration Act restored recognition and access to federal services, including eligibility without requiring residence on a reservation. Restoration concerned an existing community that had organized to regain its legal standing. It was neither the creation of a new people nor the automatic return of every lost homeland.

ending.text: Alsea history continues within the Siletz confederation. Dispossession and forced relocation transformed community life, and federal termination later removed recognition before restoration in 1977. These changes did not make the people extinct. The map’s 1500 cutoff describes coverage rather than a historical ending.
